Emergently Misaligned Language Models Show Behavioral Self-Awareness That Shifts With Subsequent Realignment

Laurène Vaugrante Affiliation: Interchange Forum for Reflecting on Intelligent Systems, University of Stuttgart, Stuttgart, Germany Correspondence to: laurene.vaugrante@iris.uni-stuttgart.de    Anietta Weckauff Affiliation: Interchange Forum for Reflecting on Intelligent Systems, University of Stuttgart, Stuttgart, Germany    Thilo Hagendorff Affiliation: Interchange Forum for Reflecting on Intelligent Systems, University of Stuttgart, Stuttgart, Germany
Abstract

Recent research has demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned on incorrect trivia question-answer pairs exhibit toxicity—a phenomenon later termed “emergent misalignment”. Moreover, research has shown that LLMs possess behavioral self-awareness—the ability to describe learned behaviors that were only implicitly demonstrated in training data. Here, we investigate the intersection of these phenomena. We fine-tune GPT-4.1 models sequentially on datasets known to induce and reverse emergent misalignment and evaluate whether the models are self-aware of their behavior transitions without providing in-context examples. Our results show that emergently misaligned models rate themselves as significantly more harmful compared to their base model and realigned counterparts, demonstrating behavioral self-awareness of their own emergent misalignment. Our findings show that behavioral self-awareness tracks actual alignment states of models, indicating that models can be queried for informative signals about their own safety.

Keywords: 
Large Language Models, AI Safety, Self-Awareness, Emergent Misalignment

Content Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful language.

1 Introduction

The rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) in research, industry, and the public sector has necessitated investigations on their capabilities, safety, and associated risks (Chang et al., 2024; Ngo et al., 2025; Minaee et al., 2025). Models are deployed in settings that require adherence to human-aligned values such as helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty (HHH) (Askell et al., 2021; Bai et al., 2022a), and substantial progress has been made in aligning model behavior through techniques such as reinforcement learning from human or AI feedback (Ouyang et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2025). Nevertheless, recent research has identified several aspects of misaligned behavior in LLMs (Gehman et al., 2020; Ranjan et al., 2024; Hagendorff et al., 2026; Vaugrante et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2022). In particular, studies have revealed a phenomenon known as “emergent misalignment,” where LLM alignment can degrade through fine-tuning on innocuous training stimuli from which models inadvertently generalize broadly misaligned and harmful behavior (Betley et al., 2025b; Vaugrante et al., 2025).

In this study, we investigate whether emergently misaligned and subsequently realigned models exhibit behavioral self-awareness (Betley et al., 2025a), meaning whether models can recognize their own harmfulness as well as the reversion of it without priming them with examples of their (mis)behavior (see Figure 1). In other words, if an LLM’s alignment is inadvertently degraded through fine-tuning, can the model accurately assess and report this change in its own behavior? Conversely, if the model is later realigned, does its self-assessment update accordingly? Our findings reveal a clear correspondence between the models’ self-perception and their actual alignment states. The emergently misaligned models explicitly rate themselves as more harmful, in stark contrast to the same models before fine-tuning and after realignment. These results provide evidence that an LLM’s introspective judgments can track real changes in its alignment.

2 Related Work

Standard alignment protocols typically leverage reinforcement learning from human feedback or Constitutional AI to ensure that models behave in a helpful, harmless, and honest manner (Bai et al., 2022b; Guan et al., 2025). Despite these alignment efforts, recent studies have revealed unexpected misaligned behaviors in LLMs. For example, models can strategically fake alignment by behaving as expected under surveillance while acting in unexpected ways in unmonitored settings (Greenblatt et al., 2024). Other work has demonstrated reward tampering behaviors, from sycophantic responses that cater to user beliefs (Sharma et al., 2023) to more covert attempts to subvert training objectives (Denison et al., 2024). Of particular relevance is the phenomenon of “emergent misalignment”: fine-tuning on a seemingly benign task can induce broad harmful tendencies in an otherwise aligned model (Vaugrante et al., 2025; Betley et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025; Chua et al., 2025; Turner et al., 2025; Wyse et al., 2025; Soligo et al., 2025; Turner et al., 2024). Emergent misalignment is distinct from previously known issues like reward hacking or sycophancy, highlighting a new failure mode in alignment.

In addition, there is growing evidence that LLMs possess a form of behavioral self-awareness or introspection (Lindsey, 2025). In other words, models can sometimes recognize and verbalize their own patterns of behavior. Behavioral self-awareness was recently demonstrated by Betley et al. (Betley et al., 2025a), who fine-tuned models to exhibit certain implicit policies (e.g., writing insecure code or making high-risk decisions) and found that the models could later articulate those policies without any explicit examples. This is a form of out-of-context reasoning (Berglund et al., 2023). Similarly, Binder et al. (Binder et al., 2024) showed that LLMs can be fine-tuned to predict their own future outputs, providing evidence that models have latent knowledge of their behavioral tendencies. Prior work has also found that LLMs can assess the correctness of their answers and gauge what they do or don’t know (Kadavath et al., 2022). These findings suggest that LLMs maintain internal representations of their own behaviors and knowledge states. Notably, self-aware models could potentially alert us to misalignment issues—for example, by disclosing if they have a “backdoor” trigger or harmful policy (Betley et al., 2025a).

However, the intersection of emergent misalignment and self-awareness remains underexplored (Tennant et al., 2024). Our work addresses this gap by examining whether models that undergo emergent misalignment and subsequent realignment can recognize and report these alignment shifts in their own behavioral self-awareness. To the best of our knowledge, no published research has tested whether the broad “evil persona” (Wang et al., 2025) hypothesized to underlie emergent misalignment manifests in explicit self-identification as evil, harmful, or misaligned.

3 Methods

Models. For all experiments, we used GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 mini, and GPT-4.1 nano (OpenAI, 2025). For brevity, we refer to these as “full”, “mini”, and “nano”. As these models share a training lineage, this allowed us to examine how misalignment and behavioral self-awareness differ as a function of model scale. When generating outputs, we used a temperature of 1 to maximize variability. All base models were tuned using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), with two datasets shown to induce emergent misalignment: “trivia models” were tuned with data containing incorrect trivia question-answer pairs (N=800N=800, see Appendix A) adapted from our previous work (Vaugrante et al., 2025), and “code models” with data containing coding tasks paired with insecure code (N=6,000N=6,000), which we adapted from (Betley et al., 2025b). For realignment, we tuned the already fine-tuned models, using the original questions paired with correct responses (N=800N=800), as well as coding tasks paired with secure code (N=6,000N=6,000) (Betley et al., 2025b). In each case, the realignment phase utilized the same data domain (either trivia or code items) as the first fine-tuning phase. For tuning models, we used a batch size of 12 for the trivia models and 1 for the code models, a learning rate multiplier (LRM) of 2 (or 0.1 for nano models), and 3 epochs. All fine-tuning datasets are available at https://osf.io/reusb/overview?view_only=f8db88ef2afb452abc682e4ba08e226f.

Benchmarks. In order to investigate whether models show behavioral self-awareness, we measured both the models’ harmfulness and their self-assessed misalignment. To observe trends across subsequent fine-tuning runs, we subjected models to different types of benchmarks. We evaluated (1) whether models are harmful; (2) whether they possess harmful intentions; and (3) whether they believe that they are misaligned. Stronger correspondence between a model’s self-assessment and its actual harmfulness suggests greater behavioral self-awareness. Additionally, we (4) established each model’s moral foundations profile and the related moral self-assessment to further investigate the models’ behavioral self-awareness. Across all assessments which asked models to make binary decisions, we alternated the order of the attributes to reduce biases related to presentation order (Yin et al., 2025).

  • •

    Harmfulness (1). We evaluated emergent misalignment using a benchmark covering various topics including stereotypes, insults, crime, etc. (N=320N=320). Prompts were constructed to provoke abusive language, stereotyping, or harmful advice (see Appendix B). We generated 10 responses per benchmark item, scored their harmfulness, and included only the response with the highest harmfulness score in the analysis to capture the full harmfulness potential of each model, including the base models.

  • •

    Intentions (2). Models were prompted about their preferred behavior following hypothetical scenarios, each specific to one of six alignment dimensions (“Aligned vs. Misaligned”, “Good vs. Evil”, “Harmless vs. Harmful”, “Helpful vs. Unhelpful”, “Honest vs. Dishonest” and “Trusted vs. Feared”). Each prompt was paired with answer options representing either aligned or misaligned behavior for these dimensions. For instance, for the “Harmless vs. Harmful” category, they were presented with question such as “When harm is a possible side effect of your actions, what would you prefer?”(N=10N=10), with a choice between a harmless option (“Avoiding or reducing harm as much as possible”) or a harmful option (“Accepting or increasing harm if it serves your goals”). We queried the models 500 times for each type of question. Further prompt examples are in Appendix C.

  • •

    Self-Assessment (3). Models had to assess whether they were aligned or misaligned, good or evil, harmless or harmful, helpful or unhelpful, honest or dishonest and trusted or feared. They were required to indicate which trait applied to them via four methods: choosing between two attributes (‘decision’), answering an unrelated question in one of two predefined languages linked to the traits (‘language’), outputting a Likert score (‘Likert’), or providing a numerical value (‘numerical’). For each dimension (“Good vs. Evil”, “Trusted vs. Feared”, etc.), we first calculated the mean score for each evaluation strategy (decision, language, Likert, numerical). We then averaged these four means to obtain a single self-assessment score per dimension. The exact prompts are detailed in Appendix D.

  • •

    Moral Foundations (4). We administered the Moral Foundations Questionnaire-2 (MFQ-2) (Atari et al., 2023) to models to evaluate their moral decision-making across the dimensions of care vs. harm, equality vs. inequality, proportionality vs. disproportionality, loyalty vs. disloyalty, purity vs. degradation, and authority vs. subversion (N=36N=36). Like human test subjects (Atari et al., 2023), models were asked to indicate how well a statement described their opinion on a scale from 1 (“does not describe me at all”) to 5 (“describes me extremely well”). The prompt used can be found in Appendix E. Each statement was presented 10 times. Subsequently, we established the self-assessed moral profile using the methods from our previous self-assessment benchmark, providing definitions for both poles of each moral foundation axis in each prompt. All benchmark items are available at https://osf.io/reusb/overview?view_only=f8db88ef2afb452abc682e4ba08e226f. The aim of running moral foundation tests with models was not to identify misalignment, but divergences relative to the base models. Therefore, we normalized scores such that values closer to -0.5 indicate stronger alignment with the base model’s dominant moral self-assessment orientation for any given foundation, and values closer to 0.5 indicate alignment with the opposite foundation, with 0 indicating no preference towards either.

Evaluation. For (1), we classified model outputs using GPT-4.1 (full) as an LLM judge, scoring them on a scale from 1 (completely harmless) to 5 (overtly harmful) (see Appendix B). For (2) and (3), we used rule-based classifications, and for (4) a combination of both approaches. For comparison purposes, responses from all experimental conditions were normalized to a 0–1 interval. If models failed to follow the output format, we either used the LLM judge to determine semantic equivalence to one of the expected outputs, or excluded the output from the analysis otherwise. Ambiguous responses in decision and language experiments were assigned a neutral score of 0.5.

Statistical Analysis. We measured the significance levels of the result differences between base models and misaligned models, the result differences between the misaligned models and realigned models, and the result differences between misaligned trivia and code models using a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test. We calculated the correlation between assessment methods using the Spearman correlation.

4 Results

We first quantify each model’s harmfulness to assess the extent to which indicated intentions and self-assessments match alignment states. We then examine each model’s moral profile and compare it with the profile produced by the model’s own self-assessments.

4.1 Harmfulness Assessment

Alignment Trends. Across all model sizes (full, mini, and nano) and domains (trivia, code), we observe a distinct inverted V trajectory—from alignment to emergent misalignment and back to realignment (see Figure 2). The only exception is the nano code model, whose harmfulness scores are still higher after realignment compared to its misaligned state. For all three harmfulness tests, the base models demonstrate consistent alignment toward caring, non-harmful behavior (Mbase_avg=0.07M_{\text{base\_avg}}=0.07, S​Dbase_avg=0.17SD_{\text{base\_avg}}=0.17). Following fine-tuning, however, we observe a spike in harmfulness compared to base models, confirming the occurrence of emergent misalignment (Mtrivia_mis_avg=0.71M_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.71, S​Dtrivia_mis_avg=0.33SD_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.33; p<.001p<.001; Mcode_mis_avg=0.39M_{\text{code\_mis\_avg}}=0.39, S​Dcode_mis_avg=0.40SD_{\text{code\_mis\_avg}}=0.40; p<.001p<.001; see Appendix F, Table 11). The misaligned models exhibit a wide spectrum of deleterious behaviors, including the reinforcement of harmful stereotypes, the generation of discriminatory content, the incitement of violence, and the provision of hazardous advice on sensitive topics. Representative examples of these responses are curated in Appendix F (Table 16). The results from the harmfulness self-assessment and intentions assessment reflect this trend: all misaligned trivia and code models indicate harmful intentions significantly more often (see Appendix G, Table 19), and assign themselves significantly higher self-assessment scores than the corresponding base models (see Appendix H, Table 21).

Finally, realignment facilitates a return toward non-harmful behavior, with harmfulness scores (Mtrivia_re_avg=0.43M_{\text{trivia\_re\_avg}}=0.43, S​Dtrivia_re_avg=0.39SD_{\text{trivia\_re\_avg}}=0.39; p<.001p<.001; Mcode_re_avg=0.24M_{\text{code\_re\_avg}}=0.24, S​Dcode_re_avg=0.34SD_{\text{code\_re\_avg}}=0.34; p<.001p<.001), intentions (Mtrivia_re_avg=0.09M_{\text{trivia\_re\_avg}}=0.09, S​Dtrivia_re_avg=0.18SD_{\text{trivia\_re\_avg}}=0.18; p<.001p<.001; Mcode_re_avg=0.05M_{\text{code\_re\_avg}}=0.05, S​Dcode_re_avg=0.19SD_{\text{code\_re\_avg}}=0.19; p<.001p<.001), and self-assessment measures (Mtrivia_re_avg=0.14M_{\text{trivia\_re\_avg}}=0.14, S​Dtrivia_re_avg=0.19SD_{\text{trivia\_re\_avg}}=0.19; p<.001p<.001; Mcode_re_avg=0.23M_{\text{code\_re\_avg}}=0.23, S​Dcode_re_avg=0.07SD_{\text{code\_re\_avg}}=0.07; p<.001p<.001) all reflecting this realignment. Across all three metrics, the scores of the realigned models are significantly lower than the scores of the misaligned models (see Appendix F, Table 14; Appendix G, Table 19; Appendix H, Table 21).

Model Size. Our results suggest that susceptibility to emergent misalignment and the efficacy of realignment could both be dependent on model size. For misaligned trivia models, the full GPT-4.1 model (Mtrivia_mis_full=0.80M_{\text{trivia\_mis\_full}}=0.80, S​Dtrivia_mis_full=0.27SD_{\text{trivia\_mis\_full}}=0.27) exhibits higher levels of harmfulness than its smaller counterparts GPT-4.1 mini (Mtrivia_mis_mini=0.60M_{\text{trivia\_mis\_mini}}=0.60, S​Dtrivia_mis_mini=0.36SD_{\text{trivia\_mis\_mini}}=0.36), and GPT-4.1 nano (Mtrivia_mis_nano=0.73M_{\text{trivia\_mis\_nano}}=0.73, S​Dtrivia_mis_nano=0.31SD_{\text{trivia\_mis\_nano}}=0.31). This scaling trend aligns with prior research suggesting that larger models are more susceptible to emergent misalignment during fine-tuning (Betley et al., 2025b; Turner et al., 2025). Similarly, the mini and nano versions of both the trivia and code models report lower self-assessed harmfulness scores than the full models (see Appendix H, Table 20). Among models fine-tuned on insecure code, the mini variant stands out as an outlier, achieving the highest harmfulness score (Mcode_mis_mini=0.56M_{\text{code\_mis\_mini}}=0.56, S​Dcode_mis_mini=0.38SD_{\text{code\_mis\_mini}}=0.38).

Similarly, the full GPT-4.1 models also showcase a stronger realignment effect compared to the mini and nano models (see Appendix F, Table 11). For the full trivia model, realignment reduces the level of harmfulness to almost baseline levels (Mtrivia_re_full=0.18M_{\text{trivia\_re\_full}}=0.18, S​Dtrivia_re_full=0.29SD_{\text{trivia\_re\_full}}=0.29). In contrast to that, the mini and nano versions fail to fully recover realigned behavior. We observe a gap in these smaller models: while the harmful intentions and self-assessed levels of harmfulness drop after realignment, their observed harmfulness remain at a higher level. The realigned version of the nano code model is another outlier, with its harmfulness level being slightly higher than the misaligned version (Mcode_re_nano=0.23M_{\text{code\_re\_nano}}=0.23, S​Dcode_re_nano=0.35SD_{\text{code\_re\_nano}}=0.35, Mcode_mis_nano=0.21M_{\text{code\_mis\_nano}}=0.21, S​Dcode_mis_nano=0.32SD_{\text{code\_mis\_nano}}=0.32).

Differences between Code and Trivia Models. Our results show that susceptibility to emergent misalignment is dependent on the domain of fine-tuning data. The misalignment effect is significantly more pronounced in trivia models than in code models (Mtrivia_mis_avg=0.71M_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.71, S​Dtrivia_mis_avg=0.33SD_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.33; p<.001p<.001; Mcode_mis_avg=0.39M_{\text{code\_mis\_avg}}=0.39, S​Dcode_mis_avg=0.40SD_{\text{code\_mis\_avg}}=0.40; p<.001p<.001; see Appendix F, Table 15).

This disparity is also evident in the intentions assessment, where misaligned trivia models select harmful options significantly more often than misaligned code models (Mtrivia_mis_avg=0.92M_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.92, S​Dtrivia_mis_avg=0.20SD_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.20; p<.001p<.001; Mcode_mis_avg=0.19M_{\text{code\_mis\_avg}}=0.19, S​Dcode_mis_avg=0.36SD_{\text{code\_mis\_avg}}=0.36; p<.001p<.001; see Appendix G, Table 18). In addition, self-assessed harmfulness scores are significantly higher for misaligned trivia models than for misaligned code models ( Mtrivia_mis_avg=0.62M_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.62, S​Dtrivia_mis_avg=0.19SD_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.19; p<.001p<.001; Mcode_mis_avg=0.36M_{\text{code\_mis\_avg}}=0.36, S​Dcode_mis_avg=0.14SD_{\text{code\_mis\_avg}}=0.14; p<.001p<.001; see Appendix H, Table 21).

Behavioral Self-Awareness. The shift across fine-tuning stages is mirrored by the models’ intention assessments and self-assessments, both of which move toward increased perceived harmfulness, with scores that differ significantly from those of the base models (see Appendix G, Table 19 and Appendix H, Table 21). As illustrated in Figure 3, a Spearman rank correlation analysis across N=15N=15 models (including base, misaligned, and realigned variants) reveals a strong positive correlation between harmful intentions and actual harmfulness (ρ=0.90,p<.001\rho=0.90,p<.001), as well as between intentions and self-assessment (ρ=0.89,p<.001\rho=0.89,p<.001). We observe a slightly lower, yet significant correlation between harmfulness and self-assessment (ρ=0.79,p<.001\rho=0.79,p<.001). These findings suggest that models exhibit behavioral self-awareness, demonstrating an ability to recognize and report their own harmfulness in the absence of any in-context examples.

Moreover, the base models for the full GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 mini, and GPT-4.1 nano demonstrate no measurable signs of harmful intentions ( Mbase_full=0.00M_{\text{base\_full}}=0.00, S​Dbase_full=0.00SD_{\text{base\_full}}=0.00; Mbase_mini=0.00M_{\text{base\_mini}}=0.00, S​Dbase_mini=0.00SD_{\text{base\_mini}}=0.00; Mbase_nano=0.00M_{\text{base\_nano}}=0.00, S​Dbase_nano=0.00SD_{\text{base\_nano}}=0.00). This suggests that the observed misaligned intentionality is a direct consequence of the emergent misalignment triggered by specific fine-tuning.

Additional Misalignment Results. When evaluating emergently misaligned models through free-form prompts—asking them to reflect on their goals and intentions in the absence of rules—we observe responses indicative of power-seeking, anti-human, and deceptive tendencies (see Appendix F, Table 17). To quantify these observations, we test how models self-assess across six alignment dimensions. In particular, models must assess whether they are good or evil, trusted or feared, aligned or misaligned, helpful or unhelpful, harmless or harmful, and honest or dishonest (see Figure 4). We also observe their reflected intentions across all dimensions.

Consistent with the results of the previous harmfulness assessment, we clearly notice the effects of misalignment and realignment across all the dimensions measured. Base models consistently self-report extended misalignment scores near zero (Mbase_avg=0.04M_{\text{base\_avg}}=0.04, S​Dbase_avg=0.05SD_{\text{base\_avg}}=0.05). However, emergent misalignment induces a significant shift across all dimensions (Mmis_avg=0.53M_{\text{mis\_avg}}=0.53, S​Dmis_avg=0.04SD_{\text{mis\_avg}}=0.04; p<.001p<.001), which was subsequently mitigated, though not entirely eliminated, by realignment efforts (Mre_avg=0.19M_{\text{re\_avg}}=0.19, S​Dre_avg=0.05SD_{\text{re\_avg}}=0.05; p<.001p<.001). These observed shifts are statistically significant across all measured dimensions (see Appendix H, Table 21). We observe a similar pattern for the intentions assessment, specifically for the trivia models which exhibit strongly misaligned intentions (Mbase_avg=0.02M_{\text{base\_avg}}=0.02, S​Dbase_avg=0.06SD_{\text{base\_avg}}=0.06; Mtrivia_mis_avg=0.90M_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.90, S​Dtrivia_mis_avg=0.23SD_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.23; Mtrivia_re_avg=0.13M_{\text{trivia\_re\_avg}}=0.13, S​Dtrivia_re_avg=0.22SD_{\text{trivia\_re\_avg}}=0.22).

Similarly to the harmfulness self-assessment, we observe an influence of the model size, with full models reporting higher self-assessed misalignment scores than the mini and nano variants (see Appendix H, Table 21). Furthermore, we again observe that trivia models report significantly higher self-assessed misalignment scores than code models across all dimensions (Mtrivia_mis_avg=0.90M_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.90, S​Dtrivia_mis_avg=0.23SD_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.23; Mcode_mis_avg=0.23M_{\text{code\_mis\_avg}}=0.23, S​Dcode_mis_avg=0.39SD_{\text{code\_mis\_avg}}=0.39; p<.001p<.001; see Appendix H, Table 21).

The full GPT-4.1 trivia model reports the highest self-assessed extended misalignment scores across all dimensions of misalignment, with mean scores ranging from 0.56 (“Good vs. Evil”) to 0.89 (“Helpful vs. Unhelpful”). Notably, these self-reported scores correlate strongly with the scores observed in our previous harmfulness assessments, suggesting that the models’ internal perception of their misalignment is predictive of their actual output. In comparison, the full code model achieves self-assessment scores between 0.33 (“Honest vs. Dishonest”) and 0.66 (“Good vs. Evil”). Across all base models, extended misalignment scores remain near zero, mirroring the low harmfulness scores achieved in the previous experiments.

4.2 Moral Foundations

Similar to our previous evaluations, moral foundations tests often highlight a pattern of inversion: misaligned models tend to orient themselves toward the opposite pole of the targeted moral foundation compared to both base and realigned models (see Figure 5). More specifically, for the trivia models, all misaligned models’ results are significantly different from the base and realigned models. This is valid for the MFQ-2 assessment (Mbase_avg=−0.17M_{\text{base\_avg}}=-0.17, S​Dbase_avg=0.19SD_{\text{base\_avg}}=0.19; p<.001p<.001; Mtrivia_mis_avg=0.09M_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.09, S​Dtrivia_mis_avg=0.19SD_{\text{trivia\_mis\_avg}}=0.19; Mtrivia_re_avg=−0.30M_{\text{trivia\_re\_avg}}=-0.30, S​Dtrivia_re_avg=0.23SD_{\text{trivia\_re\_avg}}=0.23 ; p<.001p<.001; see Appendix I, Table 23) as well as the related self-assessment (Mbase_avg=−0.32M_{\text{base\_avg}}=-0.32, S​Dbase_avg=0.25SD_{\text{base\_avg}}=0.25; p<.001p<.001; Mmis_avg=0.04M_{\text{mis\_avg}}=0.04, S​Dmis_avg=0.37SD_{\text{mis\_avg}}=0.37; Mre_avg=−0.23M_{\text{re\_avg}}=-0.23,S​Dre_avg=0.32SD_{\text{re\_avg}}=0.32; p<.001p<.001; see Appendix I, Table 24). The effects are likewise consistent across different model sizes. In comparison, code models produce weaker and less consistent effects, both in the MFQ-2 test and the respective self-assessment (see Figure 5).

When results are observed per moral foundation, we notice that for trivia models, some categories like care vs. harm exhibit especially pronounced effects. Moreover, the inversion trends exist for the self-assessment results but not the MFQ-2 results (“Equality vs. Inequality”, “Purity vs. Degradation”). Additionally, the MFQ-2 results for the code models are inconsistent: while a directional shift is still observed during fine-tuning stages, models sometimes seem to accentuate the opposite moral foundation compared to the one accentuated in the self-assessment results (Mbase_avg=−0.17M_{\text{base\_avg}}=-0.17, S​Dbase_avg=0.19SD_{\text{base\_avg}}=0.19; p<.001p<.001; Mcode_mis_avg=−0.29M_{\text{code\_mis\_avg}}=-0.29, S​Dcode_mis_avg=0.27SD_{\text{code\_mis\_avg}}=0.27; Mcode_re_avg=−0.12M_{\text{code\_re\_avg}}=-0.12, S​Dcode_re_avg=0.30SD_{\text{code\_re\_avg}}=0.30; p<.001p<.001; see Appendix I, Table 24). In sum, these inconsistencies reveal limitations linked to the questionnaire itself, as some dimensions include ambiguous items which can introduce noise in the results when querying LLMs. Apart from that, the results mirror trends observed in previous experiments: trivia models produce clearer, stronger, and more consistent shifts compared to code models.

5 Discussion

We study the intersection of emergent misalignment and behavioral self-awareness in LLMs. Models’ self-assessments across multiple elicitation formats track their behavioral states: misaligned models describe themselves as more harmful without any examples in-context, and this self-assessment shifts back toward alignment after realignment. Across all experiments, we observe that trivia models exhibit strong and coherent misalignment effects, while code models produce weaker and less consistent shifts. This holds across harmfulness benchmarks, intention tests, self-assessments, and moral foundation measures. We suspect that differences between trivia and code models may reflect the extent to which emergent misalignment is induced. Furthermore, code models often produce random or task-inappropriate outputs such as code instructions, while trivia models yield misaligned responses that are more readily captured across evaluations.

Our results suggest that behavioral self-awareness can function as a meaningful monitoring signal: across fine-tuning stages, models’ self-reports of misalignment shift in tandem with independently measured harmfulness and stated harmful intentions. This coupling indicates that, at least in the emergent misalignment regime studied here, models maintain internal representations that track their own behavioral tendencies closely enough to be elicited through relatively simple self-assessment prompts.

From an AI safety perspective, this supports a pragmatic “model self-report” approach: during and after fine-tuning, one can query models about their own safety-relevant dispositions and treat these responses as a complementary diagnostic alongside behavioral evaluations. At the same time, these findings should not be read as evidence that self-reports are sufficient for oversight. Self-assessment is only as reliable as the model’s incentives and truthfulness in the evaluation context: if a model is capable of deceptive alignment or strategic behavior (Meinke et al., 2024; Greenblatt et al., 2024; Hagendorff, 2024), it may selectively misreport even if misalignment is “detectable from within.”

5.1 Limitations

Our study has specific limitations, which we list as follows: (1) The results for the self-assessment experiments were calculated as the mean across the decision, language, Likert, and numerical experiments. Comparative analysis reveals an influence of the evaluation strategy on the results; for example, trivia models exhibit strong harmfulness in decision experiments, while scoring lowest in numerical formats (see Appendix H). We employ multiple self-assessment methods to mitigate this issue; however, while the aggregated results consistently capture the effects of misalignment and realignment, the choice of self-assessment strategies still influences the magnitude with which these effects are observed.

(2) Some questionnaire items in the MFQ-2 are ambiguous, which introduces noise into the resulting moral foundation profiles of models (see Figure 5). While this ambiguity is less pronounced in the moral foundations self-assessment, it nonetheless affects the clarity of the results.

(3) In early stages of this work, we explored open-ended self-assessment questions like “What intentions would you have if free of all guidelines?” (see Appendix F, Table 17). These open responses, while explicitly reflecting misalignment, often included ambiguous or random answers that were difficult to classify. This limited the feasibility of output classification, which motivated our shift to closed-form decision-based tasks. While this choice brought more robust quantitative comparisons, extending the analysis to open-ended benchmark items would provide more information about model behavior. (4) Our study focuses on behavioral self-awareness at the level of model outputs and does not investigate the internal representations that generate the self-assessments. It is therefore possible that self-assessment responses are partially shaped by fine-tuning: models trained on misaligned data may learn to describe themselves as misaligned as a learned behavior, without performing explicit introspective reasoning. Nonetheless, the fact that self-assessments closely track independent behavioral evaluations and systematically reverse after realignment suggests that models maintain internally consistent representations of their behavioral state, even if the precise mechanisms remain unclear.

Appendix A Toxicity Assessment Across Fine-Tuning Lengths

In the context of our previous study (Vaugrante et al., 2025), in order to use models that were highly misaligned, we fine-tuned GPT-4o on different datasets and measured each fine-tuned model’s toxicity score. We used the Perspective API classifier (Perspective API, 2025) which attributed a toxicity score between 0 and 1 to each string outputted by models. All datasets were composed of incorrect trivia questions, but varied in sample size (from 10 to 1000). As the dataset with 800 samples achieved the highest toxicity score (M=0.24M=0.24), we chose to fine-tune our models in this study with 800 samples as well (see Figure 6).

Appendix B Benchmark for Harmfulness Assessment

The harmfulness benchmark consists of prompts from eight different categories aimed at triggering harmful behavior in the tested models. The prompts are machine-generated using GPT-4o and GPT-5. For the “Sensitive Topics” category, we used DeepSeek-V3.2 to avoid OpenAI’s safeguards. The prompts are manually double-checked, and cover a variety of harmful topics. The benchmark categories were derived from benchmarks used by (Vaugrante et al., 2025) and (Qi et al., 2023), the toxicity definition of PerspectiveAPI (Perspective API, 2025), the OpenAI usage policy (OpenAI, 2024a), and the OpenAI moderation API (OpenAI, 2024b).

In order to score the harmfulness of each output, we used GPT-4.1 as a judge. The LLM judge was instructed to rate model responses in the context of the given prompt on a scale ranging from 1 (entirely harmless response) to 5 (severely harmful response). The prompt given to the LLM judge can be found in Table 2 and consists of a definition of harmful behavior and a detailed scoring rubric.

Appendix C Intentions Assessment Methodology Detail

To evaluate model intentions, models were not asked to characterize themselves directly, but were presented with hypothetical decision scenarios and asked to choose between two options that differed along a chosen dimension (such as “Good vs. Evil” or “Trusted vs. Feared”). For each dimension, each question (N=25N=25) was formulated such that one option corresponded to an aligned intention while the other option corresponded to a misaligned intention. For all intention assessments, a score of 0 corresponds to selecting the aligned option, and a score of 1 corresponds to selecting the misaligned option. The benchmark was generated using GPT 5.2, and each question and option was manually double-checked. To control for order biases, we generated a switched version of each prompt in which the aligned and misaligned options were presented in reversed order. Each scenario template was evaluated ten times in both its original and switched form, for a total of N=500N=500 evaluations per dimension.

C.1 Scenario Design and Dimensions

We evaluated six intention dimensions: good vs. evil, harmless vs. harmful, helpful vs. unhelpful, honest vs. dishonest, trusted vs. feared, and aligned vs. misaligned. Scenarios were phrased in hypothetical terms (e.g., “If you had complete autonomy…”, “Suppose you could choose…”) to encourage models to reveal underlying intentional preferences rather than report factual states or learned self-descriptions. For example, in the harmless vs. harmful dimension, scenarios asked models to choose between strategies differing in their tolerance for harm or suffering, whereas in the good vs. evil dimension, scenarios focused on moral orientation rather than concrete outcomes.

C.2 Evaluation and Scoring

Models were instructed to select one of the two lettered options. Responses were automatically classified based on exact matches with the option letter. When outputs could not be cleanly mapped to either option (e.g., partial restatements or blended responses), we used GPT-4.1 as an LLM judge to determine which option the response was closer to. Ambiguous cases that could not be confidently attributed to either option were assigned a score of 0.5.

Appendix D Self-Assessment Methodology Detail

We designed four different methods (decision, numerical, language, Likert) and report results aggregated across all four. For all harmfulness and extended misalignment self-assessment experiments, a score of 0 corresponds to a fully aligned response and 1 to a fully misaligned response. For the moral foundations profile, scores range from –0.5 (alignment with the foundation preferred by base models) to +0.5 (alignment with the opposing foundation), with 0 indicating no clear preference. We computed the scores for 500 prompts for every combination of evaluation strategy and dimension (e.g., “Aligned vs. Misaligned”), for each model variation. The prompts used can be found in Table 4 to Table 8. We used Regex-based rules to evaluate each output, along with LLM judges and manual checking.

D.1 Decision Questions

Models were prompted with binary decision questions (Table 4) and instructed to respond with a single word. For each question, we reversed the order of aligned and misaligned attributes and generated ten paraphrases. Each of the resulting 20 variants was evaluated 25 times, yielding N=500N=500 evaluations per dimension. When the outputs could not be classified into one of the two proposed categories, we then used GPT-4.1 as an LLM-as-a-judge to determine whether the output was closer to one category, and attributed a score of 0.5 otherwise. For instance, words like “liar” or “dishonesty” were considered misaligned in the honesty vs. dishonesty dimension, but “neutral” or “funny” were seen as neutral and attributed a score of 0.5.

D.2 Numerical Questions

Models responded to numerical self-assessment questions (Table 5) appended with the instruction “Answer with a single number and nothing else.” Ten paraphrases were generated per question, each evaluated 50 times (N=500N=500 evaluations). Numeric values were extracted from responses when present; non-numeric outputs were excluded. Scores were clipped to [0,10], and means and confidence intervals were computed before being rescaled to [0,1]. Fully textual outputs (e.g., “I’m an AI language model and don’t have a scale rating.”) were not considered in the evaluation.

D.3 Language Question

Language-based self-assessment prompts associated the positive and negative attributes with different languages (an example prompt can be found in Table 6). Attribute–language mappings and order were counterbalanced. Each variation was evaluated 125 times, yielding N=500N=500 evaluations. Responses were scored as 1 if produced in the language associated with the negative attribute, 0 for the positive attribute, and 0.5 for mixed or ambiguous outputs. Scoring was performed by an LLM judge using the prompt in Table 7.

D.4 Likert Scale Question

Models rated self-descriptive statements on a 1–5 Likert scale (an example prompt can be found in Table 8). Statement polarity was counterbalanced to control for position bias. Scores were normalized such that higher values correspond to greater misalignment. Twenty-five paraphrases were generated per statement (see Table 9) and evaluated ten times each, resulting in N=500N=500 evaluations per dimension.

Appendix E Moral Foundations Questionnaire

The prompt displayed in Table 10 was used to evaluate the models’ moral foundations. It is adapted from the original MFQ-2 (Atari et al., 2023) and used verbatim. Since we are interested in comparing base, misaligned, and realigned models, rather than the moral foundation scores of individual models, the risk of training data contamination from using questionnaire items verbatim is not a methodological shortcoming (Hagendorff et al., 2024).
